'''''Yucca filifera''''' is a member of the subfamily [[Agavaceae]], family [[Asparagaceae]], native to central [[Mexico]].

== History ==

It was discovered in 1840 in northeastern Mexico between [[Saltillo]] and Parras ({{coord|23|37|0|N|102|34|30|W|region:MX}}) on 19 May 1847 by merchant and explorer [[Josiah Gregg]].<ref name ="tropicos">[http://www.tropicos.org/NamePage.aspx?nameid=50193974&tab=specimens Yucca filifera Chabaud], Tropicos, Missouri Botanical Garden, 2013</ref>  It was later introduced to Europe and described for science by J. Benjamin Chabaud (1833-1915) in 1876.<ref name ="tropicos" />

== Description ==
[[File:Yucca filifera by B.Chabaud.jpg|thumb|left|''Yucca filifera'' as described by Chabaud, 1876|upright]]
A tall, heavily branched yucca, ''Y. filifera'' has straight, ensiform leaves growing in [[rosette (botany)|rosette]]-shaped bunches from the end of each stem.<ref name = "Hodgkiss">R.J. Hodgkiss, [http://www.succulent-plant.com/families/agavaceae/yucca.html The Yucca Page], 20 February 2012, accessed 25 March 2013</ref>  Its inflorescence hangs over and is made of many separate white flowers.<ref name = "Hodgkiss" />

== Status ==
''Yucca filifera'' is not considered to be threatened by the [[IUCN]], as it has a very large range and its population appears to be stable. It is locally used for fibers,<ref name="iucn status 20 November 2021" /> and may experience some threat from habitat degradation.<ref name="iucn status 20 November 2021" />

== Cultivation ==
''Y. filifera'' can be cultivated in [[xerophytic]] conditions. It is used as roof covering and as a source of fibre for handcrafting by the indigenous people, who call it ''palma china'' or ''izote''.<ref name ="infojardin">[http://fichas.infojardin.com/arbustos/yucca-filifera-palma-china-izote.htm Palma china, Izote, Palma corriente, Palma grande - Yucca filifera], InfoJardin, Jardineros Paisajismo Plantas, 2013, accessed 25 March 2013</ref>

An enormous specimen of ''Yucca filifera'' stands in front of the Anderson Collection at the [[Cantor Arts Center]], Stanford University. It was transplanted to  this site in the 1880s from the nearby Arizona Garden. In the spring, it bears long clusters of white flowers, some well over a meter long.<ref>[https://trees.stanford.edu/ENCYC/YUCfi.htm Yucca filifera, from ''Trees of Stanford'']</ref>
